analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage by $1 an hour over two years, to $6.15.
analysis.headline: The minimum wage increase bill died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or a vote, and it attracted no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $5.15 an hour to $5.65 in July 2001 and $6.15 in July 2002, a $1 increase spread over two years. It was introduced on the first day of the 107th Congress by Representative James Traficant of Ohio, sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, and then to a subcommittee. It never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and no other member signed on as a cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning at or near the federal minimum wage — then $5.15 an hour — would have seen pay rise to $5.65 by July 2001 and $6.15 by July 2002, a $1 hourly raise over two years. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers earning near the minimum wage

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.65 an hour during the year beginning July 1, 2001.
Raises it further to $6.15 an hour beginning July 1, 2002, putting an extra $1 an hour — about $2,000 a year for a full-time worker — in the pockets of the country's lowest-paid workers.
The increase is phased in over two years, giving employers time to adjust to the higher wage floor.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum wage — chiefly restaurants, retail stores, and other labor-intensive businesses — would bear higher payroll costs, some of which could be passed to consumers in higher prices. [S2][S3]

drawbacks.text: Employers of low-wage workers — especially small restaurants and retailers — would face higher payroll costs, and critics of minimum wage increases generally warn that some businesses respond by cutting hours, jobs, or raising prices.
The bill offered no offsets or accommodations for small businesses, such as a tip-credit change or tax relief, which has historically been how minimum wage bills assemble broader support.
Even the higher wage of $6.15 would have been modest; phased in over two years, part of the raise would have been eroded by inflation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is direct and easy to measure: about $2,000 a year more for a full-time worker at the minimum wage. The cost falls on the businesses that employ them, concentrated in restaurants and retail, and part of it would likely show up in prices or reduced hours. Raising the wage floor is one of the most straightforward ways to lift pay for the lowest earners, though a $1 increase phased over two years is a modest one, and the bill carried no small-business offsets that might have broadened its support. The larger problem with this particular bill was political, not substantive: with zero cosponsors, it was never positioned to go anywhere.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and died there without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Traficant introduced the bill on January 3, 2001, the first day of the 107th Congress, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
On March 2, 2001, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it sat without further action.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that pay the minimum wage are better off because the bill died, since the $1-per-hour increase never took effect. The roughly minimum-wage workers the bill would have raised pay for gain nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Minimum-wage employers who avoided the increase

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no party split is recorded; the bill also attracted no cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: These employers would have faced a legally required $1-per-hour raise for their lowest-paid workers. Their financial interest in blocking the bill ran against the workers who would have received higher pay.
Business lobbies historically press against federal minimum wage increases, arguing higher payroll costs cut jobs. The congressional record here does not show specific lobbying on this bill.
